candidate.answerReason: Karl uses 10 gallons before the stop and 5 afterward, traveling 350 + 175 = 525 miles, matching choice A.

methods.label: Track the fuel supply
methods.explanation:
Track the gas remaining at the stop to find the distance of the second part of the drive. The first \(350\) miles use \(350\div35=10\) gallons, leaving \(14-10=4\) gallons. Buying \(8\) gallons raises the supply to \(4+8=12\) gallons.

Karl finishes with half a tank, or \(14\div2=7\) gallons. He therefore uses \(12-7=5\) gallons after the stop, taking him another \(5\cdot35=175\) miles. His total distance is

\[350+175=\boxed{525\text{ miles}},\]

choice \(\mathrm{A}\).
methods.levelReason: Uses elementary fuel accounting and a fixed miles-per-gallon relationship.

candidate.annotationRationale: The target is applying a fixed quantitative relationship between fuel consumed and distance, covered by cnm_p111. The method also tracks additions to and subtractions from the fuel supply using the part-total relationships in cnm_p035.

review.mathematicalCheck: Fuel remaining progresses from 14 to 4 to 12 to 7 gallons. The second leg consumes 5 gallons and covers 175 miles, giving 525 miles total, choice A. Refueling respects tank capacity.
